properties.decision:
`ifc:core-api` moves from `published` to `internal`. The published surface is now three boundaries — `ifc:mcp-tools`, `ifc:mcp-tools-http`, `ifc:graph-export` — and every one of them passes the test: agents call the tool surfaces, and other tools and designs read the export document.

THE SAME TEST THAT SETTLED `ifc:graph-read`, applied here and failing: is anybody outside this project's control writing code against it? No. `reflow2-core` is not on crates.io, its only dependant is `reflow2-mcp` by local path in the same workspace, and users receive binaries and speak MCP rather than linking the library.

WHAT IT WAS DOING WHILE PUBLISHED, which is the concrete harm rather than a tidiness argument: `export_surface` is the document handed to another team or a vendor, and this was in it. Asked "what may I build against?", reflow2 answered with the entire Rust API of an undistributed crate — 277 public functions, described in two of nine fields.

THE UNDERLYING PROBLEM IS THAT ITS NAME IS ITS SCOPE. "DesignGraph API" means whatever that struct exposes today, and it grows whenever anyone adds a method. A contract whose scope grows by default cannot be relied on or satisfied by a second implementation. That is not fixable by writing more prose about it; the route to real contracts here is more narrow interfaces like `ifc:graph-read`, whose five operations are named and where adding a sixth is a deliberate act.

WHAT WOULD REOPEN IT — the same two triggers as `ifc:graph-read`, either sufficient: `reflow2-core` is published as a crate for others to build on, or an implementation is wanted from somebody other than this project. Neither holds today.

WHAT WAS FIXED ALONGSIDE, all of it recorded rather than silently tidied:
  — `spec` held a 2026-07-28 changelog note in place of a specification; the note is history and now lives in the change record and the snapshot, and the field describes the contract.
  — `payload_schema` read `unspecified` while eleven `schema/*.yaml` artifacts carried `SPECIFIES` edges with `format: json_schema`. The design contradicted itself about whether its own contract was written down; the field now names them.
  — `error_model`, `endpoint`, `payload_format`, `auth` and `transport_security` were unstated. All are now stated, and the last three are `none` — a fact about a library boundary with no wire, no principal and no channel, not a gap.
  — `operations` is now an explicit statement that this boundary CANNOT enumerate its operations, rather than a blank that reads as unfinished paperwork.
  — `dec:core-api-spof-accepted` named a topology that had moved; corrected, with the prior wording in `snap:epoch:v0380:dec:core-api-spof-accepted`.

🛑 ONE FINDING COULD NOT BE FIXED, AND THE REASON IS THE MORE INTERESTING RESULT. Nothing verifies this contract, and nothing verifies ANY contract in this design, because **`VERIFIES` cannot target an Interface at all**: the schema enumerates its targets as Capability, Requirement, Artifact, Component, DesignRule and Constraint. An attempt to attach `ver:store` — which does validate the eleven schema files that specify this boundary — was refused by the edge validator.

So reflow2 can check a rule, a budget, a part and a file, and cannot check a CONTRACT. Interfaces are the nodes a modular open-systems approach turns on, and they are the one kind of node the design cannot attach evidence to. That edge's own schema comments record it under-enumerating its targets TWICE before — Requirement and Constraint were each true in a real design before the list admitted it — so Interface may be the third instance of the same pattern rather than a deliberate exclusion. Left as an open question rather than fixed on the way past: widening a `to` list is a schema change and belongs to its own decision.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT CHANGED: both `sys:foundation` and `cmp:graph` provide it, and both `sys:agent-surface` and `cmp:service` consume it, which is why this one interface generated 16 of the design's declared contract pairs from what the SPOF decision calls a single path. Whether a subsystem should re-declare what its own module declares is a modelling question about levels, not a defect to repair on the way past.
properties.name: DECIDED — the DesignGraph API is withdrawn from the published surface
properties.rationale:
ANTHONY'S CALL, 2026-08-21: "go with your recommendation to fix all the findings and put internal", after a review that laid out seven findings and named which of them were judgement rather than fact.

WHY THIS IS RECORDED RATHER THAN JUST DONE. Withdrawing a published designation is a statement about what this project commits to — the opposite direction from publishing, and equally his to make. And `internal` is the DEFAULT, so a boundary sitting at it carries no evidence of whether anyone considered the question. Without this node, a later reader finds the same ambiguity that made the review necessary in the first place.

THE REVIEW ITSELF IS THE THING WORTH KEEPING, more than the answer: the test is "who outside your control writes code against this?", and it is re-applicable to every boundary rather than being a verdict about this one.
